mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about Chapter 5: Hope as a Discipline in the Face of Setbacks. If you’ve ever tried to make lasting change, you know how tough the journey can be. In abolitionist work, setbacks and slow progress aren’t just possible—they’re expected. But here’s the thing: hope isn’t just a fleeting feeling or some kind of blind optimism. It’s a discipline. It’s something you practice, especially when things get hard. So what does it really mean to treat hope as a discipline? Well, it’s about making a conscious choice to keep going, even when change feels completely out of reach. This isn’t just about believing things will get better on their own. It’s about taking action—together. Hope, in this sense, is rooted in community. When you draw strength from the people around you and from a shared purpose, it’s so much easier to keep your eyes on the bigger picture. And it’s not just about the big wins—sometimes, it’s the small victories that keep you moving. Think about those moments when progress feels tiny, almost invisible. Celebrating those steps matters. Then there’s learning from failure. Instead of letting setbacks knock you down, what if you saw them as chances to grow and adapt? Every disappointment becomes a lesson, a way to get stronger and more creative. Practicing hope also means not settling for small fixes that just patch up the surface. Sure, incremental changes can bring relief, but the real goal is to dismantle the systems causing harm in the first place. That takes patience, persistence, and a bold imagination for what’s possible. How do communities actually nurture this kind of hope? It happens through rituals and storytelling—when people gather, share what they’ve been through, mourn together, and imagine a different future. These moments remind you that you’re not alone, that you’re part of something bigger. There are a few strategies that really help keep hope alive. Regular check-ins give everyone a chance to share how they’re feeling and get the support they need. Storytelling—especially stories of resistance, survival, and transformation—can inspire and connect people across differences. And don’t underestimate the power of rest and renewal; caring for yourself and your community keeps burnout at bay. When hope becomes a discipline—an active, collective practice—movements can weather even the toughest setbacks. This isn’t passive hope; it’s a force that fuels the work of building a world where care, justice, and liberation are possible for everyone. Coming up next, we’ll dive even deeper into core abolitionist principles—exploring the challenges of reform, the power of imagination, and real steps for building a future beyond prisons and policing.
